frameworks.name: Document-Demonstrate-Duplicate
frameworks.definition: A three-stage training process: (1) Document the script and steps, (2) Demonstrate execution in front of the trainee, (3) Duplicate by watching the trainee perform and giving immediate feedback.

frameworks.name: AB Offer Architecture (Anchor + Core)
frameworks.definition: A two-tier offer structure with a high-commitment annual tier (anchor) and a shorter-term core offer; the anchor is taken by ~20% of buyers and subsidizes the blended average cash collected per door.

frameworks.name: One Avatar, One Channel, One Product
frameworks.definition: Until reaching $1M+ in revenue, a business should have exactly one customer avatar, one acquisition channel, and one core product to avoid the performance dilution of multi-front effort.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a business generating under $1M in revenue, having two avatars and five acquisition channels simultaneously causes the founder to feel spread thin and dramatically reduces the probability of succeeding at any single channel. The correct posture is one avatar, one channel, one product until that milestone is crossed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: one avatar, one channel, one product
claims.mechanism: Every additional avatar or channel splits founder attention, making it impossible to execute any single one at the level required to dominate it.
bounded_by: Does not apply once revenue crosses $1M and dedicated channel owners can be hired

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that HOA-based trash collection contracts are a commodity auction business that will always trend to lowest-bid competition, permanently compressing margins, whereas scatter residential accounts can be priced more aggressively and acquired via door-to-door with no competitive auction process.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: HOA procurement governed by competitive bid cycles
claims.mechanism: HOA procurement rules structurally require competitive bidding, which races pricing to the bottom; scatter customers make individual decisions and can be priced on perceived value rather than lowest bid.
bounded_by: HOA channel still viable for inbound deals that arrive without a competitive bid process

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies that for Philip's trash-collection business (Garby Disposal, ~2026), the binding constraint on growth is not leads or ads but cash flow: the business must collect more than $208 in the first transaction (covering $42 labor fulfillment for the first payment period plus $50 sales commission plus ~$116 bin cost) to be cash-flow positive before receiving the next quarterly payment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: cash in the first 30 days greater than cost of goods sold and CAC fully loaded
claims.mechanism: A quarterly billing cycle means the business must fund 60+ days of fulfillment out of pocket after paying sales commission and bin cost; only the first transaction can close this gap, so the first-transaction economics must be self-funding.

numbers.axis: required first-transaction cash to achieve cash-flow-positive customer acquisition

anchors.component: bin cost (financed over 10 years, but fronted)
minimum blended average to break even

bounded_by: Applies to commission-only D2D sales with quarterly billing; would differ under monthly ACH billing or company-employed salespeople

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends an AB tiered offer for Garby Disposal's door-to-door scatter customer acquisition: Offer A (anchor) is 12 months prepaid at $30/month ($360 total) with a free $99 bin; Offer B (core) is 3 months prepaid at $35/month ($105) plus $99 bin purchase, for a total of ~$189. He estimates 20% of prospects will take the $360 anchor and 80% will take the $189 core, producing a blended average of ~$270 per door, which exceeds the $208 break-even threshold.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service area with competitive alternatives around $89/quarter
claims.mechanism: An anchor offer that 20% of prospects choose adds approximately $72 of blended cash per door above the core offer alone, pushing the blended average above the cash-flow break-even line without requiring any individual transaction to cover the full $360.

numbers.axis: blended average cash collected per door sold

bounded_by: Assumes competitive market context where 3-months-free is a meaningful differentiator; may need to adjust bin price if local competitors also offer free bins

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in door-to-door residential service sales, a script limited to four questions is sufficient for a full close, and that salespeople who internalize the script and run between doors can average 10-15 sales per day, with elite performers reaching higher numbers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect already has service need (trash collection)
claims.mechanism: Short sales cycles require only qualification and closing, not extended education; a four-question script covers need identification and close, and the speed of execution means volume is the primary driver of daily income.

anchors.level: doors needed per sale (26% close rate, 30% door-open rate)

bounded_by: Assumes a residential service with low skepticism and an existing need; not applicable to high-consideration or enterprise sales

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when scaling a commission-only door-to-door sales force, using group calls rather than one-on-one interviews and offering job offers on the spot to anyone who seems normal and hardworking is the correct hiring process, because the screening criterion is hunger and work ethic, not interviewing skill.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Interview performance and work ethic are uncorrelated in commission-only field roles; a group call eliminates the worst candidates efficiently, and a job-offer-on-the-spot captures motivated applicants before they disengage.
bounded_by: Does not apply to salaried or knowledge-worker roles where interviewing skill correlates more with job performance

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in early-stage scaling of a door-to-door sales team, the founding salesperson should never canvass alone: always have a trainee shadow them so that each door knocked doubles as a training repetition, achieving a two-birds-one-stone multiplier on effort without reducing sales output.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder or lead salesperson who is also responsible for training
claims.mechanism: Simultaneous demonstration and training compresses the time-to-competence of new hires from weeks to days; trainees learn via live modeling rather than classroom instruction, which is faster for behavioral skills.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for Garby Disposal's door-to-door channel, the commission ceiling the company can offer is the primary lever for attracting higher-quality salespeople: at $50/deal, a rep making $500/day is possible; raising commission to enable $1,500/day (which requires closing ~10 deals at a higher commission) would attract an order-of-magnitude better salesperson who runs between doors and operates with sprint-level intensity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: offer economics support higher commission after offer restructuring
claims.mechanism: Commission rate determines the income ceiling for the rep, which determines the quality of candidate the role attracts; higher income ceiling selects for candidates with proven track record of high daily volume.

numbers.axis: daily income ceiling and corresponding rep quality

bounded_by: Only viable after offer restructuring generates enough margin to support higher commission per deal

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in commission-only door-to-door hiring for service businesses, married men with children outperform single men without dependents because financial necessity converts into higher sustained effort; the candidate's personal circumstances, not interviewing performance, predict commission-only field sales outcomes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Financial obligations eliminate the option to stop working; the behavioral driver is necessity rather than ambition, making performance more consistent under adverse conditions (cold weather, rejection streaks).
bounded_by: Correlation, not causation; individual exceptions exist; does not apply to salaried roles where compensation is decoupled from output

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that with Garby Disposal's existing close rate (26% door-open rate x 26% close = 1 sale per ~12 doors), deploying 10 commissioned-only reps averaging conservatively 5 deals per day produces 50 deals per day, 1,500 per month, and roughly 18,000 new customers per year — overshooting Philip's stated 3,000-customer profitability threshold by approximately 6x.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Linear scaling of a proven per-rep output rate (5 deals/day) across a team of 10 reps produces compounding territory penetration without increasing overhead proportionally.

numbers.axis: monthly new customer acquisition at different team sizes

bounded_by: Assumes territory density supports 10 concurrent reps without saturation; territory limits may bind before 18,000 units

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the Document-Demonstrate-Duplicate training loop — where the trainer (1) has the trainee memorize the script while walking between doors, (2) demonstrates closing in front of the trainee, and (3) rides shotgun while the trainee closes and receives immediate feedback — is the fastest way to compress time-to-competence for door-to-door salespeople compared to classroom-based training.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: behavioral skill that repeats in a short cycle (2-minute sales interaction)
claims.mechanism: Immediate feedback loops (feedback given between doors, not after a day or week) match the behavioral science principle that reinforcement closest in time to the behavior produces the fastest learning.
bounded_by: Less effective for complex multi-call B2B sales where the feedback loop is weeks long

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for cold-outreach acquisition of HOA accounts in a market where approximately 70% of households are governed by HOAs, targeted handwritten personal letters delivered at a rate of 1-2 per day is the correct channel — not cold email, which exhausts the small list too quickly.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B service sold to HOA property managers
claims.mechanism: A list of 500 accounts on 3-year contract cycles yields approximately 150 renewal opportunities per year; at 1-2 contacts per day, a single founder can maintain full coverage of the addressable list with a high-touch medium that differentiates from email spam.

numbers.axis: HOA outreach cadence vs. list exhaustion

bounded_by: For HOA markets larger than a few thousand, cold email becomes more viable because list size no longer depletes quickly

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when building a paid-ad creative strategy for a local service business, recording 10 different versions of the highest-performing video ad (with different shirts, backgrounds, props, and locations) produces more usable test variations at lower marginal cost than producing new concepts from scratch.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: local service business running Meta/Facebook ads
one proven winning creative already exists

numbers.axis: number of creative variations from one winning concept

anchors.approach: multi-variation shoot (different shirts, backgrounds, truck, neighbor)

bounded_by: Hormozi immediately notes this is secondary to door-to-door for Philip's specific stage; paid ads are the growth channel after the core offer and team are in place

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the correct ad script structure for a local service business leads with customer pain (the specific frustrations the prospect experiences with their current provider) before introducing the business owner's name and credentials, because prospects have zero prior context and are motivated by their own problems, not the seller's identity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: leading more with the things that they're interested in
claims.mechanism: Cold audiences have no reason to care about the business owner's name until they recognize the pain is being addressed; leading with pain establishes relevance before asking for attention.
bounded_by: In warm or retargeted audiences, brand recognition may warrant a different opening sequence

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that offering a price-escalation path for customers who provide their own service equipment (e.g., their own trash bin) — specifically charging a higher ongoing rate to customers who opt out of the company-supplied bin — is a valid pricing lever because the company has one-sided information (it knows the actual cost is trivial) and the customer perceives the bin as high-value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business that bundles equipment with service
equipment has low actual depreciation cost but high perceived value
claims.mechanism: The customer has no visibility into the operator's equipment cost; offering the equipment as an upgrade at a price far above depreciation captures margin from information asymmetry without lying.

anchors.offered_price: $99 upfront (buy-out) or financing over 3 years at ~$150

anchors.perceived_customer_value: enough that most pay without objection

bounded_by: Does not apply when competitors offer the same equipment for free, which shifts the reference price to zero

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for Garby Disposal, the fastest path to profitability is the single simplest set of necessary beliefs: if 10 commissioned-only door-to-door reps can be recruited and each averages 5 deals per day, the math solves. Every additional assumption (ads, HOA strategy, pricing optimization) is additive noise that reduces the probability the core thesis executes. The goal is to identify the minimum-assumption path to the target.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: early-stage business that has proven a single acquisition channel works
founder has limited time and capital to run multiple experiments simultaneously
claims.mechanism: Each additional assumption in a business plan multiplies the probability of failure; the minimum-assumption path has the highest probability of execution, even if it is not the theoretically optimal path.
bounded_by: Does not mean never test secondary channels; means test them only after the primary channel is proven and systemized

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a local service business operator adds a QR-code or advertising sticker to service equipment left in the customer's property, it should be paired with an opt-out upgrade fee (e.g., $5/month to remove the QR code), because a majority of customers will not care enough to pay to remove it, and the few who do effectively subsidize a price increase for the whole base.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business that leaves branded equipment on customer property
customer has low aesthetic sensitivity to branding on equipment
bounded_by: Philip's specific customer base values clean aesthetics (gray bins) and may have a higher opt-out rate than average

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a business's cash flow constraint — not its marketing, ads, or product — is the correct first problem to solve when the unit economics show a positive LTV-to-CAC ratio but the business is cash-flow negative. For Garby Disposal (LTV:CAC of 20:1), the problem was not lead generation but that the billing cycle created a gap between acquisition cost and cash collection that burned capital every month.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business with a favorable LTV:CAC ratio (>3:1)
claims.mechanism: A 20:1 LTV:CAC ratio means the business model is sound at maturity; a negative cash flow means the timing of cash collection does not cover the timing of cash outflows. The correct fix is to change billing structure, not to generate more leads or reduce price.

numbers.axis: LTV:CAC ratio vs. cash flow health

bounded_by: Applies when LTV:CAC is already proven positive; if the LTV:CAC itself is below 3:1, the problem is the business model, not billing timing

examples.text: Philip (Garby Disposal Services, Virginia, ~2026) left a software engineering role at Amazon to start a residential trash collection business. After nearly two years of 16-hour days, the business generated $642,000 in revenue with a net loss of $151,000 (negative 23% net margin) and 2,500 customers. The primary cash drain was a quarterly billing model that required the business to front a $42 fulfillment cost plus a $50 sales commission and $116 bin cost per new customer before receiving the second quarterly payment. Alex Hormozi diagnosed this as a cash timing problem rather than a demand problem, noting the scatter segment had a 20:1 LTV-to-CAC ratio and 0.4% monthly churn — both excellent fundamentals masked by the billing structure.

Philip's existing door-to-door channel showed a 30% door-open rate and a 26% close rate among opened doors, meaning roughly 1 sale per 12 doors knocked. Philip's first commissioned rep, three weeks into the role, was already averaging 5-7 deals per day. Hormozi used this data point to argue that the entire growth thesis could be executed by recruiting 10 such reps on commission-only, requiring no additional capital allocation to paid channels, no product changes, and no HOA strategy.

Philip's existing Meta ad creative — a selfie-style video where Philip introduced himself and described Garby Disposal's service before listing customer pain points — was his highest-performing ad. Hormozi noted the video worked because it felt authentic and locally specific, but recommended flipping the script to lead with pain points (rising prices, unreliable pickups) before the personal introduction, because cold-audience prospects have no prior reason to care about the founder's name before recognizing their own problem.

Philip had been running a three-months-free promotional offer to overcome the price objection from incumbents. Hormozi restructured this into an AB offer: the anchor (12-month prepay at $30/month = $360, free $99 bin) and the core (3-month prepay at $35 = $105 plus $99 bin purchase = $189 total). Both offers include three months free. The key insight was that the 20% who take the anchor contribute $72 of blended cash per door above the core offer alone, pushing the average above the $208 break-even threshold without requiring the core offer to fully cover all costs.

practices.text: Place a QR code or contact sticker on every service bin left on customer property to convert passive equipment into an active lead generation asset. Pair with an opt-out fee to monetize the placement directly.

For commission-only field sales hiring, run group video calls (2 minutes per candidate) rather than individual interviews, then invite those who seem normal and hardworking to meet in person and offer jobs on the spot.

Write Indeed and Craigslist job ads for commission-only field reps to the rep's perspective: lead with their income ceiling and daily schedule flexibility, include a damaging admission about physical conditions (heat, cold), and exclude education requirements. Attract based on hunger and earning potential, not credentials.

For door-to-door service sales training, set up a door at the facility and drill the opener until the rep can deliver it in their sleep before going to the field. Run role-plays where the rep must handle common objections (spouse objection, card not available) until responses are automatic.
Add ACH as a payment option and incentivize customers to switch via a small gift card, because ACH reduces card-decline operational overhead and improves reliability of recurring billing.

For HOA outreach in a market of ~500 HOAs on 3-year cycles, visit 1-2 HOA managers per day (or dedicate one day per week to 7 visits) with handwritten cards and personal gifts rather than cold email, which depletes the small list too quickly and fails to differentiate.

Lead salesperson should always canvass with a trainee so that every sales call is simultaneously a training repetition; pass lead-trainer status to the trainee once they become the best salesperson, and pay $10 more per deal for the additional complexity of carrying a shadow.
